title: Deep Learning Foundations
subtitle: Every question from the study guide: Lectures 1–6 and NumPy

questions.title: Core: Inputs of the hypothesis function
questions.text: What are the inputs to the hypothesis function h_θ? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: It receives the input features: a vector x, or a matrix X for a batch of examples.
It receives the model parameters θ (also written as weights W and biases b).
It receives the ground-truth label y as one of its inputs.
It receives the loss value J(θ) as one of its inputs.

questions.explanation: The hypothesis is h_θ(x). Its inputs are the features and the parameters. The label and the loss are not inputs to h_θ.

questions.title: Core: Outputs of the hypothesis function
questions.text: What are the outputs (the value) of the hypothesis function? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: In regression the output is a continuous value, or a vector of continuous values.
In binary classification the output is an estimated probability P(y=1|x) in [0, 1], or a class label after thresholding.
In multi-class classification the output is a probability distribution over classes, a vector that sums to 1.
In regression the output is restricted to a discrete class label.
In multi-class classification the output is one unbounded scalar.

questions.explanation: The hypothesis outputs a prediction ŷ. Regression is continuous, binary classification is a probability or a thresholded label, and multi-class classification is a distribution over classes.

questions.title: Core: Format of a label
questions.text: What can be the format of a label? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: A label can be a scalar, as in single-target regression (y in R) or binary classification (y in {0, 1}).
A label can be a vector, as in multi-output regression, multi-label classification, or a one-hot multi-class label.
A label can be a matrix or tensor, as in a segmentation mask or a video annotation.
A label must always be a scalar in {0, 1}.

questions.explanation: Supervised labels can be scalars, vectors, or matrices/tensors. They are not restricted to a single binary scalar.

questions.title: Core: Constituents of a supervised data point
questions.text: What are the constituents of a data point in supervised learning? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: A data point is an input feature vector x = [x_1, ..., x_n]^T together with its ground-truth label y.
A supervised data point is only an unlabeled feature vector x.
A supervised data point is a reward and the next state, with no label.

questions.explanation: Supervised learning pairs features x with a target y. Unlabeled x belongs to unsupervised learning, and a reward belongs to reinforcement learning.

questions.title: Core: Role of the loss function
questions.text: What is the role of the loss function? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: It measures the discrepancy between the prediction ŷ = h_θ(x) and the true target y.
Averaged over a dataset it is the cost J(θ), and it guides learning.
It replaces the hypothesis and directly stores the training features.
Its role is to be maximized so that the predictions become arbitrarily large.

questions.explanation: The loss penalizes the gap between prediction and target. The dataset-level objective J(θ) is what optimization minimizes.

questions.title: Core: Shape of the loss value
questions.text: Can the value of the loss function be a scalar, a vector, or a matrix? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: The final cost J(θ) is always a scalar, so that it can be minimized.
Individual sample losses in a batch may form a vector before they are reduced by averaging or summing.
The objective J(θ) itself is a matrix, with one row per parameter.
The objective J(θ) itself is a vector, with one entry per class.

questions.explanation: J(θ) is a single real number. A batch can hold per-example losses in a vector, but that vector is reduced before it becomes the objective.

questions.title: Core: Reinforcement learning feedback
questions.text: In reinforcement learning, what feedback comes from the environment, and how does it differ from supervised learning? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: Reinforcement learning feedback is a numerical reward, often delayed, sparse, and evaluative rather than instructive.
A reward says how good or bad an action was. It does not name the correct action.
Supervised learning gives an explicit ground-truth label for every training example.
Reinforcement learning provides the correct action for every state, in the same way a label does.
Supervised learning feedback is only a delayed scalar reward.

questions.explanation: Rewards evaluate an action. Labels instruct the model with the correct target. Those are different kinds of feedback.

questions.title: Tasks: Task types
questions.text: Which statements about these learning tasks are TRUE?

options.text: Regression is supervised. Its goal is to predict a continuous value from input features.
Classification is supervised. Its goal is to predict a discrete class label.
Clustering is unsupervised. Its goal is to group unlabeled data by similarity.
Dimensionality reduction is unsupervised. Its goal is to compress data while keeping important structure, as PCA does.
Denoising reconstructs a clean signal from a noisy input. It can be supervised, self-supervised, or unsupervised.
Clustering is supervised and requires a class label for every point.

questions.explanation: Regression and classification use labels. Clustering and dimensionality reduction do not. Denoising can sit in more than one of those settings.

questions.title: Tasks: Linear regression: task and supervision
questions.text: Is linear regression used for regression or classification? Is it supervised or unsupervised? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: Linear regression is used for regression.
Linear regression is supervised.
Linear regression is used for classification.
Linear regression is unsupervised.

questions.explanation: Linear regression predicts a continuous target from labeled examples.

questions.title: Tasks: Logistic regression: task and supervision
questions.text: Is logistic regression used for regression or classification? Is it supervised or unsupervised? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: Logistic regression is used for classification, despite the word regression in its name.
Logistic regression is supervised.
Logistic regression is used to predict an unbounded continuous target.
Logistic regression is unsupervised.

questions.explanation: The name is misleading: logistic regression classifies labeled examples.

questions.title: Cholesterol: Linear or logistic regression
questions.text: We want to predict cholesterol, a continuous value, from weight, age, height, and sex (n = 4 features) using m = 200 patients. Which model should we use? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: Use linear regression, because the target is a continuous number.
Use logistic regression, because cholesterol is a class label.

questions.explanation: A continuous target calls for linear regression, not logistic regression.

questions.title: Cholesterol: Number of parameters
questions.text: We want to predict cholesterol, a continuous value, from weight, age, height, and sex (n = 4 features) using m = 200 patients. How many parameters θ does linear regression with a bias term have? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: There are 5 parameters: one weight for each of the 4 features, plus a bias θ_0.
There are 4 parameters, one per feature, and no bias.
There are 200 parameters, one per patient.

questions.explanation: θ = (θ_0, θ_1, θ_2, θ_3, θ_4). The bias is an extra parameter, and the patient count is not the parameter count.

questions.title: Cholesterol: Loss function
questions.text: We want to predict cholesterol, a continuous value, from weight, age, height, and sex (n = 4 features) using m = 200 patients. Which loss should we use? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: Use mean squared error (least squares).
Use binary cross-entropy, because the target is continuous.

questions.explanation: Least squares / MSE is the loss for this continuous target.

questions.title: Cholesterol: Shape of X in the matrix hypothesis
questions.text: We want to predict cholesterol, a continuous value, from weight, age, height, and sex (n = 4 features) using m = 200 patients. For h_θ(X) = Xθ, with a column of ones in X, which statements about the shape of X are TRUE?

options.text: X has shape (200, 5), that is (m, n + 1).
X has shape (200, 4), because the bias column is not included.
X has shape (5, 200).

questions.explanation: 200 patients and 4 features plus the intercept column give X a shape of (200, 5).

questions.title: Cholesterol: Shape of θ in the matrix hypothesis
questions.text: We want to predict cholesterol, a continuous value, from weight, age, height, and sex (n = 4 features) using m = 200 patients. For h_θ(X) = Xθ, which statements about the shape of θ are TRUE?

options.text: θ has shape (5, 1). A 1D array of length 5 is the same parameter vector.
θ has shape (200, 1).
θ has shape (4, 1), with no bias entry.

questions.explanation: θ is (n + 1) by 1, so (5, 1).

questions.title: Cholesterol: Shape of h_θ(X)
questions.text: We want to predict cholesterol, a continuous value, from weight, age, height, and sex (n = 4 features) using m = 200 patients. For h_θ(X) = Xθ, which statements about the shape of h_θ(X) are TRUE?

options.text: h_θ(X) has shape (200, 1).
h_θ(X) has shape (200, 5).
h_θ(X) has shape (5, 1).

questions.explanation: X is (200, 5) and θ is (5, 1), so the product is (200, 1).

questions.title: Cholesterol: Range of h_θ(X)
questions.text: We want to predict cholesterol, a continuous value, from weight, age, height, and sex (n = 4 features) using m = 200 patients. For h_θ(X) = Xθ, which statements about the range of values in h_θ(X) are TRUE?

options.text: Every entry can be any real number, so the range is (−∞, +∞).
Every entry lies in (0, 1).
Every entry lies in {0, 1}.

questions.explanation: A linear prediction is unbounded.

questions.title: Cholesterol: Where patient age is stored
questions.text: We want to predict cholesterol, a continuous value, from weight, age, height, and sex (n = 4 features) using m = 200 patients. Are the patients' ages inside θ or inside X? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: Ages are inside X. They are feature values.
Ages are inside θ. They are learned parameters.

questions.explanation: Patient measurements are data, so they live in X, not in θ.

questions.title: Cholesterol: Do we minimize X?
questions.text: We want to predict cholesterol, a continuous value, from weight, age, height, and sex (n = 4 features) using m = 200 patients. Do we minimize X during learning? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: No. X is fixed training data.
Yes. Learning updates the entries of X.

questions.explanation: The feature matrix is given. Training does not minimize it.

questions.title: Cholesterol: Do we minimize h_θ(X)?
questions.text: We want to predict cholesterol, a continuous value, from weight, age, height, and sex (n = 4 features) using m = 200 patients. Do we minimize h_θ(X) during learning? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: No. Minimizing the predictions themselves would push them toward arbitrarily low values.
Yes. The goal is to make every cholesterol prediction as small as possible.

questions.explanation: We want accurate predictions, not the smallest possible predictions.

questions.title: Cholesterol: Do we minimize θ?
questions.text: We want to predict cholesterol, a continuous value, from weight, age, height, and sex (n = 4 features) using m = 200 patients. Do we minimize θ during learning? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: No. Minimizing θ itself is not the goal. Regularization can penalize large weights, but learning minimizes the loss.
Yes. Gradient descent minimizes the parameter vector θ directly.

questions.explanation: The objective is J(θ), not the size of θ. A regularizer only adds a penalty on large weights.

questions.title: Cholesterol: What do we minimize?
questions.text: We want to predict cholesterol, a continuous value, from weight, age, height, and sex (n = 4 features) using m = 200 patients. What do we minimize during learning? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: We minimize the cost J(θ), for example the mean squared error.
We minimize the feature matrix X.
We minimize the predictions h_θ(X).
We minimize the parameter vector θ by itself.

questions.explanation: Training minimizes the loss J(θ). It does not minimize X, the predictions, or θ directly.

questions.title: Cholesterol: Scalar hypothesis: vector or scalar
questions.text: We want to predict cholesterol, a continuous value, from weight, age, height, and sex (n = 4 features) using m = 200 patients. For one patient, h_θ(x) = θ^T x = sum_i θ_i x_i. Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: h_θ(x) is a scalar: one predicted cholesterol value.
h_θ(x) is a vector with one entry per feature.

questions.explanation: The dot product θ^T x collapses to a single number.

questions.title: Cholesterol: Range of the scalar hypothesis
questions.text: We want to predict cholesterol, a continuous value, from weight, age, height, and sex (n = 4 features) using m = 200 patients. What is the range of h_θ(x) = θ^T x? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: The range is (−∞, +∞).
The range is (0, 1).

questions.explanation: A linear function of the features is unbounded.

questions.title: Cholesterol: Age assigned to θ or x
questions.text: We want to predict cholesterol, a continuous value, from weight, age, height, and sex (n = 4 features) using m = 200 patients. For a single patient, is age assigned to θ or to x? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: Age is assigned to a feature value x_i.
Age is assigned to a parameter θ_i.

questions.explanation: Age is an observed feature, so it is a component of x.

questions.title: Cholesterol: Geometry with one input
questions.text: For linear regression, what is the geometric picture with one input variable plotted on (x, y) axes? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: The hypothesis is a straight line, y = θ_1 x_1 + θ_0.
The hypothesis is a circle in the (x, y) plane.

questions.explanation: One feature plus a bias is a line.

questions.title: Cholesterol: Geometry with two inputs
questions.text: For linear regression, what is the geometric picture with two input variables plotted on (x_1, x_2, y) axes? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: The hypothesis is a flat plane in 3D space.
The hypothesis is a curved paraboloid.

questions.explanation: Two features plus a bias define a plane, not a curved surface.

questions.title: Cholesterol: Normal equation: shape of X
questions.text: The normal equation is θ = (X^T X + λ I)^{-1} X^T y, for the same cholesterol problem (m = 200, n = 4, with a bias). Which statements about the shape of X are TRUE?

options.text: X has shape (200, 5).
X has shape (5, 200).

questions.explanation: X is still the design matrix with 200 rows and 5 columns.

questions.title: Cholesterol: Normal equation: shape of y
questions.text: The normal equation is θ = (X^T X + λ I)^{-1} X^T y, for the same cholesterol problem (m = 200, n = 4, with a bias). Which statements about the shape of y are TRUE?

options.text: y has shape (200, 1).
y has shape (5, 1).

questions.explanation: There is one cholesterol target per patient, so y is (200, 1).

questions.title: Cholesterol: Normal equation: shape of θ
questions.text: The normal equation is θ = (X^T X + λ I)^{-1} X^T y, for the same cholesterol problem (m = 200, n = 4, with a bias). Which statements about the shape of θ are TRUE?

options.text: θ has shape (5, 1).
θ has shape (200, 1).

questions.explanation: The solved parameter vector has one entry per column of X, so (5, 1).

questions.title: Cholesterol: Where the cholesterol levels go
questions.text: The normal equation is θ = (X^T X + λ I)^{-1} X^T y, for the same cholesterol problem (m = 200, n = 4, with a bias). Where are the cholesterol levels placed? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: They are placed in the target vector y.
They are placed in the parameter vector θ.
They are placed in the identity matrix I.

questions.explanation: Cholesterol is the target, so it is y. θ holds parameters and I is the identity used for regularization.

questions.title: Cholesterol: What the I matrix is
questions.text: The normal equation is θ = (X^T X + λ I)^{-1} X^T y, for the same cholesterol problem (m = 200, n = 4, with a bias). What is the I matrix? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: I is the identity matrix, of size (n + 1) by (n + 1), here 5 by 5.
The top-left entry is typically I_0,0 = 0, so the bias is not regularized.
I stores the patient features.
I is the 200 by 200 matrix of cholesterol levels.

questions.explanation: I is the 5×5 identity used in the ridge term. Zeroing I_0,0 leaves the bias unpenalized.

questions.title: Cholesterol: Global optimum for linear regression
questions.text: With a small enough step size, is gradient descent guaranteed to find the globally optimal parameters of linear regression with mean squared error? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: Yes. Linear regression with MSE is strictly convex: one global minimum and no local minima.
No. This loss has many local minima, so a small step size is not enough.

questions.explanation: MSE on a linear model is strictly convex, so gradient descent reaches the global optimum.

questions.title: Cholesterol: Global optimum for an MLP
questions.text: With a small enough step size, is gradient descent guaranteed to find the globally optimal parameters of a multi-layer perceptron trained with mean squared error? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: No. The loss of a neural network is non-convex, so gradient descent can stop at a local minimum or a saddle.
Yes. A small enough step size guarantees the global optimum, just as it does for linear regression.

questions.explanation: An MLP is not a convex problem. A small learning rate does not remove local minima or saddles.

questions.title: Scaling: Purpose of feature scaling
questions.text: What is the purpose of feature scaling? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: It puts features on comparable numeric ranges, so the loss contours are rounder instead of long thin ellipses.
It speeds up gradient descent and stops a feature with a huge magnitude from dominating.
It changes the labels so that a convex loss becomes non-convex.
It removes the need for a loss function.

questions.explanation: Scaling is about the geometry of the loss in parameter space. It does not replace the loss or relabel the data.

questions.title: Scaling: Training without feature scaling
questions.text: What happens if we do not use feature scaling? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: Gradient descent can zigzag, converge much more slowly, or diverge when the learning rate is too large.
The optimization path is unchanged, because the scale of a feature never matters.

questions.explanation: Uneven feature scales stretch the loss contours, which makes gradient descent inefficient or unstable.

questions.title: Scaling: Min-max scaling and outliers
questions.text: Which is more robust to outliers, min-max scaling or standardization? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: Standardization, z = (x − μ) / σ, is more robust to outliers.
Min-max scaling uses x_min and x_max, so one extreme outlier squeezes the rest of the data into a tiny interval.
Min-max scaling is more robust to outliers than standardization.

questions.explanation: Min-max depends directly on the most extreme values. Standardization uses the mean and standard deviation and is the more robust of the two.

questions.title: Diagnosis: Linear or logistic regression
questions.text: We want to classify patients as sick or healthy from 2 blood-test values (n = 2) using m = 100 patients. The model is logistic regression, h_θ(X) = g(Xθ), with g(z) = 1 / (1 + e^(−z)). Which model fits this problem? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: Use logistic regression.
Use linear regression, because sick versus healthy is a continuous target.

questions.explanation: Sick versus healthy is a binary label, so the model is logistic regression.

questions.title: Diagnosis: Number of parameters
questions.text: We want to classify patients as sick or healthy from 2 blood-test values (n = 2) using m = 100 patients. The model is logistic regression, h_θ(X) = g(Xθ), with g(z) = 1 / (1 + e^(−z)). How many parameters does logistic regression with a bias have? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: There are 3 parameters: the bias θ_0 and the two weights θ_1 and θ_2.
There are 2 parameters and no bias.
There are 100 parameters, one per patient.

questions.explanation: Two features plus a bias give 3 parameters.

questions.title: Diagnosis: Loss function
questions.text: We want to classify patients as sick or healthy from 2 blood-test values (n = 2) using m = 100 patients. The model is logistic regression, h_θ(X) = g(Xθ), with g(z) = 1 / (1 + e^(−z)). Which loss is the standard choice? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: Binary cross-entropy, also called log loss or negative log-likelihood.
Mean squared error is the standard loss for this classification task.

questions.explanation: Binary classification with logistic regression uses binary cross-entropy.

questions.title: Diagnosis: Shape of X
questions.text: We want to classify patients as sick or healthy from 2 blood-test values (n = 2) using m = 100 patients. The model is logistic regression, h_θ(X) = g(Xθ), with g(z) = 1 / (1 + e^(−z)). Which statements about the shape of X are TRUE? X includes the bias column.

options.text: X has shape (100, 3).
X has shape (100, 2), because the bias column is omitted.
X has shape (3, 100).

questions.explanation: 100 patients and 2 features plus a bias column give (100, 3).

questions.title: Diagnosis: Shape of θ
questions.text: We want to classify patients as sick or healthy from 2 blood-test values (n = 2) using m = 100 patients. The model is logistic regression, h_θ(X) = g(Xθ), with g(z) = 1 / (1 + e^(−z)). Which statements about the shape of θ are TRUE?

options.text: θ has shape (3, 1).
θ has shape (100, 1).

questions.explanation: There is one parameter per column of X, so θ is (3, 1).

questions.title: Diagnosis: Shape of h_θ(X)
questions.text: We want to classify patients as sick or healthy from 2 blood-test values (n = 2) using m = 100 patients. The model is logistic regression, h_θ(X) = g(Xθ), with g(z) = 1 / (1 + e^(−z)). Which statements about the shape of h_θ(X) are TRUE?

options.text: h_θ(X) has shape (100, 1).
h_θ(X) has shape (100, 3).

questions.explanation: There is one probability per patient, so the result is (100, 1).

questions.title: Diagnosis: Range of h_θ(X)
questions.text: We want to classify patients as sick or healthy from 2 blood-test values (n = 2) using m = 100 patients. The model is logistic regression, h_θ(X) = g(Xθ), with g(z) = 1 / (1 + e^(−z)). Which statements about the range of h_θ(X) are TRUE?

options.text: The values lie in (0, 1). They are probabilities.
The values lie in (−∞, +∞).

questions.explanation: The sigmoid squashes the linear score into (0, 1).

questions.title: Diagnosis: Where the blood-test results are stored
questions.text: We want to classify patients as sick or healthy from 2 blood-test values (n = 2) using m = 100 patients. The model is logistic regression, h_θ(X) = g(Xθ), with g(z) = 1 / (1 + e^(−z)). Are the blood-test results in θ or in X? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: They are in X.
They are in θ.

questions.explanation: Blood-test values are features, so they are columns of X.

questions.title: Diagnosis: What we minimize
questions.text: We want to classify patients as sick or healthy from 2 blood-test values (n = 2) using m = 100 patients. The model is logistic regression, h_θ(X) = g(Xθ), with g(z) = 1 / (1 + e^(−z)). What do we minimize during learning? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: We minimize the binary cross-entropy cost J(θ).
We minimize the feature matrix X.
We minimize the parameter vector θ itself.
We minimize the predictions h_θ(X).
We minimize the sigmoid function g.

questions.explanation: The objective is J(θ). We do not minimize X, θ, h_θ(X), or g.

questions.title: Diagnosis: Scalar hypothesis: vector or scalar
questions.text: For one patient, h_θ(x) = g(θ^T x). Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: h_θ(x) is a scalar.
h_θ(x) is a vector with one entry per feature.

questions.explanation: g is applied to one logit, so the result is a single probability.

questions.title: Diagnosis: Range of the logit
questions.text: For h_θ(x) = g(θ^T x), what is the range of the logit z = θ^T x? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: The logit z lies in (−∞, +∞).
The logit z lies in (0, 1).

questions.explanation: The linear score is unbounded. The sigmoid is what maps it into (0, 1).

questions.title: Diagnosis: Range of the scalar hypothesis
questions.text: For h_θ(x) = g(θ^T x), what is the range of h_θ(x)? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: h_θ(x) lies in (0, 1).
h_θ(x) lies in (−∞, +∞).

questions.explanation: The sigmoid output is a probability in (0, 1).

questions.title: Diagnosis: Blood tests assigned to x or θ
questions.text: For a single patient, where are the blood-test results assigned? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: They are assigned to feature values x_i.
They are assigned to parameters θ_i.

questions.explanation: A blood-test result is an observed feature, so it is a component of x.

questions.title: Losses: Mean squared error
questions.text: Which statements about mean squared error are TRUE? The formula in the study guide is J(θ) = (1/(2m)) * sum_i (h_θ(x^(i)) − y^(i))^2.

options.text: That formula is the mean squared error used for regression.
m is the number of training examples, and i indexes those examples.
J(θ) evaluates to a scalar.
This is the standard loss for multi-class classification.
J(θ) evaluates to a vector with one entry per example, and that vector is the objective.

questions.explanation: MSE is a regression loss. m counts examples, i indexes them, and the summed objective is a scalar.

questions.title: Losses: Binary cross-entropy
questions.text: Which statements about binary cross-entropy are TRUE? The formula is J(θ) = −(1/m) * sum_i [ y^(i) log(h_θ(x^(i))) + (1 − y^(i)) log(1 − h_θ(x^(i))) ].

options.text: That formula is binary cross-entropy.
It is the loss for binary classification.
It is the loss for an unbounded continuous regression target.

questions.explanation: Binary cross-entropy matches a binary label. Regression uses MSE instead.

questions.title: Losses: Categorical cross-entropy
questions.text: Which statements about categorical cross-entropy are TRUE? The formula is J(θ) = −(1/m) * sum_i sum_k y_k^(i) log(ŷ_k^(i)).

options.text: That formula is categorical cross-entropy.
It is the loss for multi-class classification, and k indexes the classes.
It is the loss for a single continuous target.

questions.explanation: The inner sum over k compares a one-hot (or class) label with the predicted class probabilities.

questions.title: Losses: Regularization term
questions.text: Which statements about the regularization term (λ/(2m)) * sum_{j=1}^{n} θ_j^2 are TRUE?

options.text: j indexes the feature weights and starts at 1, so the bias θ_0 is excluded.
The term penalizes large feature weights.
The sum includes the bias term θ_0.
j indexes training examples rather than parameters.

questions.explanation: The regularizer sums θ_j^2 over feature weights only. The bias, j = 0, is left out, and j is not an example index.

questions.title: MLP: Parameters in the first layer
questions.text: A 2-layer MLP is h(x) = g_2(W_2 · g_1(W_1 x + b_1) + b_2). It regresses one continuous output from 20 inputs, with 10 hidden neurons. Which statements about the first layer (W_1, b_1) are TRUE?

options.text: W_1 is 10 by 20, so it has 200 weights.
b_1 has 10 biases, one per hidden neuron.
The first layer has 210 parameters in total.
The first layer has 20 parameters, one per input.

questions.explanation: Each of 10 hidden units has 20 incoming weights and 1 bias: 200 + 10 = 210.

questions.title: MLP: Parameters in the second layer
questions.text: A 2-layer MLP is h(x) = g_2(W_2 · g_1(W_1 x + b_1) + b_2). It regresses one continuous output from 20 inputs, with 10 hidden neurons. Which statements about the second layer (W_2, b_2) are TRUE?

options.text: W_2 is 1 by 10, so it has 10 weights.
b_2 has 1 bias.
The second layer has 11 parameters in total.
W_2 is 10 by 20.

questions.explanation: The output neuron reads 10 hidden units, so W_2 has 10 weights plus 1 bias.

questions.title: MLP: Total number of parameters
questions.text: A 2-layer MLP is h(x) = g_2(W_2 · g_1(W_1 x + b_1) + b_2). It regresses one continuous output from 20 inputs, with 10 hidden neurons. How many trainable parameters does the whole network have? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: The network has 221 parameters, because 210 + 11 = 221.
The network has 200 parameters.
The network has 30 parameters.

questions.explanation: Layer 1 contributes 210 parameters and layer 2 contributes 11.

questions.title: MLP: Omitting the hidden activation
questions.text: A 2-layer MLP is h(x) = g_2(W_2 · g_1(W_1 x + b_1) + b_2). It regresses one continuous output from 20 inputs, with 10 hidden neurons. Should we omit the hidden activation g_1? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: No. Omitting g_1 collapses the network into a linear model.
Yes. Removing g_1 makes the model more flexible.

questions.explanation: Without a nonlinearity between the layers, the two linear maps compose into one linear map.

questions.title: MLP: Omitting the output activation
questions.text: A 2-layer MLP is h(x) = g_2(W_2 · g_1(W_1 x + b_1) + b_2). It regresses one continuous output from 20 inputs, with 10 hidden neurons. Should we omit g_2 for this regression task? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: Yes. Omit g_2, or use the identity g_2(z) = z, so the output can be any real number.
No. g_2 must be a nonlinearity, otherwise a continuous target cannot be predicted.

questions.explanation: Regression needs an unbounded output. The identity, or no g_2, provides that.

questions.title: MLP: Sigmoid as the regression output
questions.text: A 2-layer MLP is h(x) = g_2(W_2 · g_1(W_1 x + b_1) + b_2). It regresses one continuous output from 20 inputs, with 10 hidden neurons. Should g_2 be a sigmoid? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: No. A sigmoid would restrict the output to (0, 1), which cannot represent an arbitrary continuous target.
Yes. A regression output should pass through a sigmoid.

questions.explanation: Sigmoid is for a probability, not for an unbounded regression target.

questions.title: MLP: Binary classification head
questions.text: For binary classification with this MLP, which statements are TRUE?

options.text: The output layer has 1 neuron.
g_2 should be a sigmoid.
The loss should be binary cross-entropy.
g_2 should be a softmax over K output neurons.

questions.explanation: One sigmoid neuron plus binary cross-entropy is the binary-classification head.

questions.title: MLP: Multi-class classification head
questions.text: For multi-class classification with K classes, which statements are TRUE?

options.text: The output layer has K neurons.
g_2 should be softmax.
The loss should be categorical cross-entropy.
The output layer has 1 neuron and uses a sigmoid.

questions.explanation: K-way classification uses K logits, a softmax, and categorical cross-entropy.

questions.title: MLP: Sigmoid activation
questions.text: Which statements about the sigmoid activation are TRUE?

options.text: σ(z) = 1 / (1 + e^(−z)), its range is (0, 1), and its graph is an S-shaped curve.
The range of sigmoid is (−1, 1).

questions.explanation: Sigmoid maps every real input into the open interval (0, 1).

questions.title: MLP: Tanh activation
questions.text: Which statements about the tanh activation are TRUE?

options.text: tanh(z) = (e^z − e^(−z)) / (e^z + e^(−z)), its range is (−1, 1), and it is a zero-centered S-curve.
The range of tanh is (0, 1).

questions.explanation: Tanh is the zero-centered S-curve with outputs in (−1, 1).

questions.title: MLP: ReLU activation
questions.text: Which statements about ReLU are TRUE?

options.text: ReLU is max(0, z). Its range is [0, +∞): 0 for z ≤ 0, and a line of slope 1 for z > 0.
ReLU is max(αz, z), with a nonzero slope for negative inputs.

questions.explanation: ReLU clamps negatives to 0. The negative slope belongs to Leaky ReLU, not ReLU.

questions.title: MLP: Leaky ReLU activation
questions.text: Which statements about Leaky ReLU are TRUE?

options.text: Leaky ReLU is max(αz, z). Its range is (−∞, +∞), with a small slope α for z < 0.
Leaky ReLU outputs 0 for every negative input.

questions.explanation: The leak αz keeps a small gradient for negative inputs, so the range is all real numbers.

questions.title: Overfitting: Fewer training examples
questions.text: How does decreasing the number of training examples affect overfitting? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: Overfitting becomes more severe.
Overfitting becomes less severe.

questions.explanation: With fewer training examples, the model has less evidence and overfits more easily.

questions.title: Overfitting: More training examples
questions.text: How does increasing the number of training examples affect overfitting? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: Overfitting decreases.
Overfitting increases.

questions.explanation: More training data makes it harder for the model to memorize noise.

questions.title: Overfitting: Fewer test examples
questions.text: How does decreasing the number of test examples affect overfitting? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: The severity of overfitting does not change. Test-set size only changes the variance of the evaluation metric.
Fewer test examples make the trained model overfit more.

questions.explanation: Overfitting is a property of the trained model. The test set is only used to measure it.

questions.title: Overfitting: More parameters
questions.text: How does increasing the number of model parameters affect overfitting? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: Overfitting increases, because the model has more capacity to memorize noise.
Overfitting decreases, because extra parameters always generalize better.

questions.explanation: Higher capacity makes memorization easier, so the overfitting risk goes up.

questions.title: Overfitting: Fewer parameters
questions.text: How does decreasing the number of model parameters affect overfitting? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: Overfitting decreases.
Overfitting increases.

questions.explanation: A smaller model has less capacity to fit noise.

questions.title: Overfitting: Purpose of early stopping
questions.text: What is the purpose of early stopping? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: It limits overfitting by stopping training before the model fits noise in the training set.
Its purpose is to drive the training loss as low as possible, even after the validation loss starts rising.

questions.explanation: Early stopping trades a lower training loss for better generalization.

questions.title: Overfitting: When to stop training
questions.text: When should early stopping halt training? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: Stop when the validation loss stops improving and keeps increasing.
Stop when the training loss starts to increase.

questions.explanation: The signal is the validation loss, not the training loss.

questions.title: Overfitting: Stopping on a rising training loss
questions.text: Should we stop when the training loss begins to increase? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: No. Training loss usually keeps falling. What matters is the validation loss.
Yes. A rising training loss is the early-stopping rule.

questions.explanation: Training loss is not the early-stopping monitor. Validation loss is.

questions.title: Overfitting: Validation loss up, training loss down
questions.text: What does it mean when validation loss increases while training loss decreases? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: The model is overfitting.
The model is underfitting.

questions.explanation: The model is still fitting the training set while getting worse on held-out data. That is overfitting.

questions.title: Overfitting: Parameters and hyperparameters
questions.text: Which statements about parameters and hyperparameters are TRUE?

options.text: Parameters such as W and b are learned by gradient-based optimizers such as SGD or Adam.
Hyperparameters such as the learning rate, the number of layers, and the batch size are set before training.
Hyperparameters are chosen by a search, such as grid search, random search, or Bayesian optimization, not by gradient descent on the training loss.
The learning rate is a parameter that SGD updates together with the weights.

questions.explanation: Weights and biases are trained. Learning rate, depth, and batch size are chosen outside the gradient update.

questions.title: Overfitting: Pure SGD
questions.text: Which statements about pure SGD are TRUE?

options.text: Pure SGD uses batch size 1 and computes the gradient from a single training example on each step.
Pure SGD uses the entire training set on every step.

questions.explanation: Pure SGD means one example per update. Using the full set is batch gradient descent.

questions.title: Overfitting: Increasing the batch size
questions.text: Compared with pure SGD, what happens when the batch size increases? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: Gradient estimates become less noisy, so the trajectory is smoother.
Hardware is used more efficiently, because more of the work can run in parallel on a GPU.
An epoch takes fewer steps, but each step is more expensive.
Gradient estimates become noisier as the batch gets larger.

questions.explanation: A larger batch averages more examples. That reduces noise and uses the device better, at a higher cost per step.

questions.title: Overfitting: Decreasing the batch size
questions.text: What happens when the batch size decreases? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: Gradient steps get noisier, which can help the optimizer leave sharp minima.
The memory footprint gets smaller.
An epoch gets slower because matrix parallelism is used less well.
A smaller batch always uses more memory than a larger batch.

questions.explanation: Smaller batches add noise, use less memory, and make poorer use of parallel hardware.

questions.title: Backprop: Chain rule
questions.text: Which statement of the chain rule, as used on a computational graph, is TRUE?

options.text: ∂J/∂x = (∂J/∂output) · (∂output/∂x).
∂J/∂x = ∂J/∂output + ∂output/∂x.

questions.explanation: Backpropagation multiplies the upstream gradient by the local derivative. It does not add them.

questions.title: Backprop: Square node
questions.text: For a square node c = b^2, with grad_c = ∂J/∂c, which statements are TRUE?

options.text: grad_b = grad_c · 2b.
grad_b = grad_c · 2c.

questions.explanation: ∂c/∂b = 2b, so the upstream gradient is multiplied by 2b. Multiplying by 2c is the wrong local derivative.

questions.title: Backprop: Addition node
questions.text: For an addition node c = a + b, with grad_c = ∂J/∂c, which statements are TRUE?

options.text: grad_a = grad_c and grad_b = grad_c.
grad_a = grad_c + b and grad_b = grad_c + a.

questions.explanation: ∂c/∂a and ∂c/∂b are both 1, so both inputs receive the upstream gradient unchanged.

questions.title: NumPy attributes: Can shape be (5, 6)?
questions.text: my_array is a numpy.ndarray. Can my_array.shape be (5, 6)? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: Yes. (5, 6) is a valid shape for a 2D array.
No. A shape cannot be a tuple of two integers.

questions.explanation: shape is a tuple. (5, 6) describes a 2-dimensional array.

questions.title: NumPy attributes: Can shape be (1,)?
questions.text: Can my_array.shape be (1,)? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: Yes. (1,) is a 1D array with one element.
No. A shape tuple must contain at least two entries.

questions.explanation: A one-element tuple is a valid 1D shape.

questions.title: NumPy attributes: Can shape be (0, 1, 0)?
questions.text: Can my_array.shape be (0, 1, 0)? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: Yes. (0, 1, 0) is a valid 3D shape, and the array has zero elements.
No. A dimension of a shape is not allowed to be zero.

questions.explanation: NumPy allows zero-size dimensions. (0, 1, 0) is a legal empty 3D array.

questions.title: NumPy attributes: Can shape be the integer 12?
questions.text: Can my_array.shape be 12? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: No. shape is always a tuple, for example (12,), never a bare integer.
Yes. shape can be the integer 12.

questions.explanation: shape is a tuple. The 1D shape with 12 elements is (12,), not 12.

questions.title: NumPy attributes: Can dtype be (5, 6)?
questions.text: Can my_array.dtype be (5, 6)? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: No. dtype is a data type, such as float64 or int32, not a shape.
Yes. dtype stores the array's shape.

questions.explanation: dtype describes the element type. The shape is a different attribute.

questions.title: NumPy attributes: Can size be (5, 6)?
questions.text: Can my_array.size be (5, 6)? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: No. size is a scalar integer, the total number of elements.
Yes. size can be a tuple such as (5, 6).

questions.explanation: size counts elements. It is not a tuple. The tuple (5, 6) would be a shape.

questions.title: NumPy attributes: Can size be 12?
questions.text: Can my_array.size be 12? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: Yes. An array of shape (3, 4), for example, has size 12.
No. size must be a tuple.

questions.explanation: size is the product of the dimensions, so (3, 4) has size 12.

questions.title: NumPy attributes: Can ndim be (5, 6)?
questions.text: Can my_array.ndim be (5, 6)? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: No. ndim is a scalar integer, the number of axes.
Yes. ndim stores the shape tuple.

questions.explanation: ndim is the length of the shape, not the shape itself. A shape (5, 6) has ndim 2.

questions.title: NumPy slicing: Shape of my_array[:, :]
questions.text: Let my_array have shape (32, 5). Which statements about my_array[:, :] are TRUE?

options.text: The result has shape (32, 5).
The result has shape (32,).

questions.explanation: Slicing every row and every column keeps the original shape.

questions.title: NumPy slicing: Shape of my_array[:, 1]
questions.text: Let my_array have shape (32, 5). Which statements about my_array[:, 1] are TRUE?

options.text: The result has shape (32,). An integer index drops that axis.
The result has shape (32, 1). The indexed axis is kept.

questions.explanation: Indexing column 1 with an integer removes that axis, leaving one value per row.

questions.title: NumPy slicing: Shape of my_array[1, :]
questions.text: Let my_array have shape (32, 5). Which statements about my_array[1, :] are TRUE?

options.text: The result has shape (5,). An integer index drops that axis.
The result has shape (1, 5).

questions.explanation: Indexing row 1 with an integer returns that row as a 1D array of length 5.

questions.title: NumPy slicing: Shape of my_array[1:, :]
questions.text: Let my_array have shape (32, 5). Which statements about my_array[1:, :] are TRUE?

options.text: The result has shape (31, 5).
The result has shape (32, 5).

questions.explanation: The slice 1: drops only the first row, so 31 rows remain and all 5 columns stay.

questions.title: NumPy slicing: Shape of my_array[0, :-1]
questions.text: Let my_array have shape (32, 5). Which statements about my_array[0, :-1] are TRUE?

options.text: The result has shape (4,).
The result has shape (1, 4).

questions.explanation: Row 0 is selected with an integer, and :-1 keeps 4 of the 5 columns, so the result is 1D with length 4.

questions.title: NumPy slicing: Shape of my_array[[0], :]
questions.text: Let my_array have shape (32, 5). Which statements about my_array[[0], :] are TRUE?

options.text: The result has shape (1, 5). A list index keeps the axis.
The result has shape (5,), because any row selection drops the axis.

questions.explanation: Indexing with the list [0] is fancy indexing, so the row axis is preserved as length 1.

questions.title: NumPy slicing: Shape of my_array[[-1, -1], -1]
questions.text: Let my_array have shape (32, 5). Which statements about my_array[[-1, -1], -1] are TRUE?

options.text: The result has shape (2,). It selects the last column at rows −1 and −1.
The result has shape (2, 5).

questions.explanation: The row index picks two rows (both the last row) and the integer column index drops the column axis, leaving 2 elements.

questions.title: NumPy broadcasting: my_array1 + my_array2
questions.text: Let my_array1 have shape (32, 5) and a numeric dtype. my_array2 has shape (32,) where it is mentioned. For my_array1 + my_array2, which statements are TRUE?

options.text: It raises ValueError. The trailing dimensions 5 and 32 cannot be broadcast together.
It succeeds and the result has shape (32, 5).

questions.explanation: Aligning (32, 5) with (32,) compares 5 against 32 on the last axis, and those sizes disagree.

questions.title: NumPy broadcasting: my_array1 + my_array2[:, None]
questions.text: Let my_array1 have shape (32, 5) and a numeric dtype. my_array2 has shape (32,) where it is mentioned. my_array2[:, None] has shape (32, 1). For my_array1 + my_array2[:, None], which statements are TRUE?

options.text: It does not raise ValueError, and the result has shape (32, 5).
It raises ValueError because 32 and 5 disagree.
It succeeds, but the result has shape (32, 1).

questions.explanation: (32, 1) broadcasts across the 5 columns of (32, 5), so the sum has shape (32, 5).

questions.title: NumPy broadcasting: my_array1 + my_array2[None, :]
questions.text: Let my_array1 have shape (32, 5) and a numeric dtype. my_array2 has shape (32,) where it is mentioned. my_array2[None, :] has shape (1, 32). For my_array1 + my_array2[None, :], which statements are TRUE?

options.text: It raises ValueError, because the dimension 32 does not match 5.
It succeeds and the result has shape (32, 5).

questions.explanation: The last axes are 5 and 32. Neither is 1, and they are not equal, so broadcasting fails.

questions.title: NumPy broadcasting: my_array1 + 1
questions.text: Let my_array1 have shape (32, 5) and a numeric dtype. my_array2 has shape (32,) where it is mentioned. For my_array1 + 1, which statements are TRUE?

options.text: It does not raise ValueError. A scalar broadcasts to any shape.
It raises ValueError, because a scalar has no shape to align.

questions.explanation: Scalars broadcast to every element, so adding 1 is valid.

questions.title: NumPy reductions: Shape of my_array < 0
questions.text: Let my_array have shape (32, 5). Which statements about my_array < 0 are TRUE?

options.text: The result has shape (32, 5) and is a boolean array.
The result has shape (32,), with one boolean per row.

questions.explanation: Comparison is elementwise, so the boolean array keeps the original shape.

questions.title: NumPy reductions: Shape of my_array.T
questions.text: Let my_array have shape (32, 5). Which statements about my_array.T are TRUE?

options.text: The result has shape (5, 32).
The result has shape (32, 5).

questions.explanation: Transpose swaps the two axes.

questions.title: NumPy reductions: Shape of my_array.T.T
questions.text: Let my_array have shape (32, 5). Which statements about my_array.T.T are TRUE?

options.text: The result has shape (32, 5).
The result has shape (5, 32).

questions.explanation: Transposing twice returns the original axis order.

questions.title: NumPy reductions: Shape of my_array + my_array
questions.text: Let my_array have shape (32, 5). Which statements about my_array + my_array are TRUE?

options.text: The result has shape (32, 5).
The result has shape (64, 5).

questions.explanation: Adding an array to itself is elementwise and does not change the shape.

questions.title: NumPy reductions: Shape of my_array + my_array[:, None, :]
questions.text: Let my_array have shape (32, 5). my_array[:, None, :] has shape (32, 1, 5). Which statements about my_array + my_array[:, None, :] are TRUE?

options.text: The result has shape (32, 32, 5). The shapes (32, 5) and (32, 1, 5) broadcast to that.
The result has shape (32, 1, 5).
It raises ValueError.

questions.explanation: (32, 5) is aligned on the right as (32, 5) against (32, 1, 5). The new middle axis expands from 1 to 32.

questions.title: NumPy reductions: Shape of np.mean on axis 0
questions.text: Let my_array have shape (32, 5). Which statements about np.mean(my_array, axis=0) are TRUE?

options.text: The result has shape (5,). Axis 0 is collapsed.
The result has shape (32,).

questions.explanation: Averaging over axis 0 removes the 32 rows and leaves the 5 columns.

questions.title: NumPy reductions: Shape of np.mean on axis 1
questions.text: Let my_array have shape (32, 5). Which statements about np.mean(my_array, axis=1) are TRUE?

options.text: The result has shape (32,). Axis 1 is collapsed.
The result has shape (5,).

questions.explanation: Averaging over axis 1 removes the 5 columns and leaves one mean per row.

questions.title: NumPy reductions: Type of a sum over an axis
questions.text: Let my_array have shape (32, 5). Will type(np.sum(my_array, axis=0)) be numpy.ndarray? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: Yes. Summing over one axis still returns a numpy.ndarray.
No. Any call to np.sum returns a NumPy scalar.

questions.explanation: Keeping an axis in the output means the result is still an array, here of shape (5,).

questions.title: NumPy reductions: Type of a sum over the whole array
questions.text: Let my_array have shape (32, 5). Will type(np.sum(my_array)) be numpy.ndarray? Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: No. A sum with no axis returns a NumPy scalar, such as np.int64 or np.float64.
Yes. np.sum always returns a numpy.ndarray.

questions.explanation: Reducing every axis leaves a 0-dimensional NumPy scalar, not an ndarray.

questions.title: NumPy transforms: Shape of the reshaped arange
questions.text: Let my_array = np.arange(4).reshape(2, -1), so my_array is [[0, 1], [2, 3]] with shape (2, 2). Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: my_array has shape (2, 2).
my_array contains [[0, 1], [2, 3]].
my_array has shape (4,).

questions.explanation: np.arange(4) is [0, 1, 2, 3], and reshape(2, -1) makes a 2 by 2 matrix.

questions.title: NumPy transforms: Shape of my_array * 2 + 1
questions.text: Let my_array = np.arange(4).reshape(2, -1), so my_array is [[0, 1], [2, 3]] with shape (2, 2). Which statements about my_array * 2 + 1 are TRUE?

options.text: The result has shape (2, 2).
The result has shape (4,).

questions.explanation: Scaling and adding a scalar are elementwise, so the shape stays (2, 2).

questions.title: NumPy transforms: Shape of a positive mask
questions.text: Let my_array = np.arange(4).reshape(2, -1), so my_array is [[0, 1], [2, 3]] with shape (2, 2). Which statements about my_array[my_array > 0] are TRUE?

options.text: The result has shape (3,). Boolean masking flattens the selected elements into 1D.
The result has shape (2, 2).

questions.explanation: The entries greater than 0 are 1, 2, and 3. Boolean indexing returns them as a 1D array.

questions.title: NumPy transforms: Shape of the positive even mask
questions.text: Let my_array = np.arange(4).reshape(2, -1), so my_array is [[0, 1], [2, 3]] with shape (2, 2). Which statements about my_array[(my_array > 0) & (my_array % 2 == 0)] are TRUE?

options.text: The result has shape (1,). The only matching value is 2.
The result has shape (2,), because both 2 and 0 match.

questions.explanation: 0 is even but not positive. 1 and 3 are positive but odd. Only 2 satisfies both tests.

questions.title: NumPy transforms: Broadcast with reshape(2, 2, -1)
questions.text: Let my_array = np.arange(4).reshape(2, -1), so my_array is [[0, 1], [2, 3]] with shape (2, 2). Which statements about my_array * my_array.reshape(2, 2, -1) are TRUE?

options.text: reshape(2, 2, -1) has shape (2, 2, 1), and multiplying by my_array of shape (2, 2) broadcasts to (2, 2, 2).
The product has shape (2, 2).
The product raises ValueError.

questions.explanation: (2, 2) aligns to the right of (2, 2, 1) and expands the last axis from 1 to 2, giving (2, 2, 2).

questions.title: NumPy views: reshape returns a view
questions.text: Let my_array = np.arange(4). After my_array2[:] = 99, is the original my_array affected? my_array2 = my_array.reshape(2, 2). Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: Yes. reshape returns a view, so writing into my_array2 also changes my_array.
No. reshape returns a copy, so my_array is unchanged.

questions.explanation: reshape shares the original data buffer when it can return a view.

questions.title: NumPy views: transpose returns a view
questions.text: Let my_array = np.arange(4). After my_array2[:] = 99, is the original my_array affected? my_array2 = my_array.T. Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: Yes. Transpose returns a view, so writing into my_array2 also changes my_array.
No. Transpose always copies the data.

questions.explanation: The transpose is another view of the same buffer.

questions.title: NumPy views: np.append returns a copy
questions.text: Let my_array = np.arange(4). After my_array2[:] = 99, is the original my_array affected? my_array2 = np.append(my_array, 42). Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: No. np.append allocates a new array, so my_array is unchanged.
Yes. np.append returns a view of my_array.

questions.explanation: append cannot extend the original buffer in place, so the result is a new array.

questions.title: NumPy views: A basic slice is a view
questions.text: Let my_array = np.arange(4). After my_array2[:] = 99, is the original my_array affected? my_array2 = my_array[1:2]. Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: Yes. Basic slicing returns a view, so writing into my_array2 also changes my_array.
No. A slice such as 1:2 always copies the data.

questions.explanation: A slice with a colon is a view, not a copy.

questions.title: NumPy views: Fancy indexing copies
questions.text: Let my_array = np.arange(4). After my_array2[:] = 99, is the original my_array affected? my_array2 = my_array[[1, 2]]. Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: No. Indexing with an integer list copies the data, so my_array is unchanged.
Yes. The list [1, 2] is a basic slice and returns a view.

questions.explanation: Integer-array indexing, also called fancy indexing, returns a copy.

questions.title: NumPy views: Boolean indexing copies
questions.text: Let my_array = np.arange(4). After my_array2[:] = 99, is the original my_array affected? my_array2 = my_array[my_array < 2]. Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: No. Boolean indexing returns a copy, so my_array is unchanged.
Yes. A boolean mask returns a view.

questions.explanation: Selecting with a mask gathers elements into a new array.

questions.title: NumPy views: Arithmetic returns a new array
questions.text: Let my_array = np.arange(4). After my_array2[:] = 99, is the original my_array affected? my_array2 = my_array + my_array. Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: No. Arithmetic returns a new array, so my_array is unchanged.
Yes. my_array + my_array is a view of my_array.

questions.explanation: Adding two arrays allocates the result. It does not alias the inputs.

questions.title: NumPy functions: count_nonzero of zeros
questions.text: Let my_array = np.arange(4).reshape(2, -1), so my_array is [[0, 1], [2, 3]]. Which statements about np.count_nonzero(my_array == 0) are TRUE?

options.text: The result is 1.
The result is 0, because the array has no zeros.
The result is 4.

questions.explanation: The matrix contains a single 0, in the top-left entry.

questions.title: NumPy functions: any zero
questions.text: Let my_array = np.arange(4).reshape(2, -1), so my_array is [[0, 1], [2, 3]]. Which statements about np.any(my_array == 0) are TRUE?

options.text: The result is True.
The result is False.

questions.explanation: There is at least one zero, so np.any of the comparison is True.

questions.title: NumPy functions: all zeros along axis 1
questions.text: Let my_array = np.arange(4).reshape(2, -1), so my_array is [[0, 1], [2, 3]]. Which statements about np.all(my_array == 0, axis=1) are TRUE?

options.text: The result is array([False, False]).
The result is array([True, False]), because the first row starts with 0.

questions.explanation: Neither row is entirely zero. The first row is [0, 1] and the second is [2, 3].

questions.title: NumPy functions: unique values
questions.text: Let my_array = np.array([3, 1, 2]). Which statements about np.unique(my_array) are TRUE?

options.text: The result is array([1, 2, 3]). Unique values are returned in sorted order.
The result is array([3, 1, 2]), the original order.

questions.explanation: np.unique sorts the distinct values, so 1, 2, 3 come out in that order.

questions.title: NumPy functions: unique of a comparison
questions.text: Let my_array = np.array([3, 1, 2]). Which statements about np.unique(my_array == 0) are TRUE?

options.text: The result is array([False]). Every element is nonzero, so the comparison is all False.
The result is array([True, False]).

questions.explanation: 3, 1, and 2 are all nonzero. The boolean array has only False, and unique keeps that one value.

questions.title: NumPy functions: bincount
questions.text: Let my_array = np.array([3, 1, 2]). Which statements about np.bincount(my_array) are TRUE?

options.text: The result is array([0, 1, 1, 1]). It counts how often the indices 0, 1, 2, and 3 occur.
The result is array([1, 1, 1]), one count for each stored value.

questions.explanation: There is no 0, one 1, one 2, and one 3, so the counts are [0, 1, 1, 1].

questions.title: NumPy functions: sort reversed
questions.text: Let my_array = np.array([3, 1, 2]). Which statements about np.sort(my_array)[::-1] are TRUE?

options.text: The result is array([3, 2, 1]).
The result is array([1, 2, 3]).

questions.explanation: np.sort returns [1, 2, 3], and reversing that slice gives [3, 2, 1].

questions.title: NumPy functions: argsort
questions.text: Let my_array = np.array([3, 1, 2]). Which statements about np.argsort(my_array) are TRUE?

options.text: The result is array([1, 2, 0]). Value 1 is at index 1, value 2 is at index 2, and value 3 is at index 0.
The result is array([0, 1, 2]).

questions.explanation: argsort returns positions in ascending value order, not the values themselves.

questions.title: NumPy functions: Mask of nonzero entries
questions.text: Let my_array = np.array([3, 1, 2]). Which statements about my_array[my_array != 0] are TRUE?

options.text: The result is array([3, 1, 2]).
The result is an empty array, because the mask removes every element.

questions.explanation: None of 3, 1, or 2 is zero, so the mask keeps every element in the original order.
